summary: Reserves an additional, larger IPv6 prefix, a /20, for use in documentation, expanding on 2001:db8::/32 from RFC 3849. This lets examples reflect realistic deployments for large networks. It updates RFC 3849.

eli5.summary: Writers use pretend addresses in examples. This sets aside a bigger block of pretend addresses so big-network examples fit.

questions: what ipv6 prefix is for documentation
what does rfc 9637 change in rfc 3849
subtitle: Reserves 3fff::/20 as a second, much larger IPv6 block for documentation examples.

tldr.problem: The documentation prefix 2001:db8::/32 from RFC 3849 is too small to describe many realistic IPv6 deployments, so writers borrow real address space.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9637 reserves an additional /20 prefix from the Global Unicast Address pool for documentation; IANA registered it as 3fff::/20.
tldr.outcome: Examples can show large networks without clashing with real allocations, as long as the prefix is never used for real traffic.

today: RFC 9637 is an Informational document that updates RFC 3849, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a Bigger Documentation Prefix
sections.content:
RFC 3849 reserved 2001:db8::/32 for documentation, to reduce the chance of conflict and confusion between examples and deployed systems. IPv6 networks have since grown in size and diversity, and the RFC says the original block is inadequate for many realistic scenarios.

Without more space, documentation prefixes are drawn from blocks already allocated to organizations or well-known ISPs, or from the unallocated pool. That conflicts with existing or future allocations. Reserving a /20 from the Global Unicast Address pool avoids this.
sections.eli5: If the pretend-address box is too small, writers grab real addresses by mistake. A bigger box stops that.

sections.title: Why a /20
sections.content:
Using Regional Internet Registry data from August 2023, the RFC notes that 25.9% of the 62,770 recorded IPv6 unicast allocations and assignments were larger than a /32. The most common size was a /29, at 24.8%.

The four largest end-user assignments have been /19s, but they predate the RIRs moving away from a fixed /48 site prefix. It is unlikely that individual networks will need more than a /20 in the foreseeable future, so a /20 is believed to cover documentation needs.
sections.eli5: The authors looked at how big real networks are and picked a block big enough for nearly all of them.

sections.title: Filtering and Appropriate Use
sections.content:
Documentation prefixes are for configuration and documentation examples. They MUST NOT be used for actual traffic, MUST NOT be globally advertised, and SHOULD NOT be used internally for routed production traffic or other connectivity.

They should be treated as bogons and filtered in routing advertisements as appropriate.
sections.eli5: These are pretend addresses. Never send real mail to them, and tell nobody they are real.

sections.title: Security and the IANA Entry
sections.content:
The prefix should be considered bogon, and packets whose source or destination belongs to it should be dropped and disallowed over the public Internet.

IANA registered address block 3fff::/20, named Documentation, in the IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registry, with an allocation date of 2024-07 and Source, Destination, Forwardable, Globally Reachable and Reserved-by-Protocol all set to False.
sections.eli5: Routers should throw away anything using these pretend addresses, and the official list now records the new block.

references.text: Huston, G., Lord, A., and P. Smith, "IPv6 Address Prefix Reserved for Documentation", RFC 3849, July 2004.
Hinden, R. and S. Deering, "IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture", RFC 4291, February 2006.
